NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION)
The intervention is a thermally-symmetric cell interconnect design that equalizes heat distribution across the module. Standard practice uses uniform busbars that do not address thermal gradients, leading to uneven cell temperatures and accelerated capacity fade. This mitigation departs by using a thermally-conductive interconnect with integrated thermal vias that create a lateral heat distribution path between cells, equalizing temperatures without active cooling. The closest existing practice is thermal management systems using phase-change materials or liquid cooling, which require external hardware and energy input; this intervention passively equalizes temperatures through the interconnect structure alone, using existing materials in a novel configuration.

PHYSICS CHECK
The governing relation is the temperature-dependent capacity fade rate: dC/dt = A·exp(-Ea/RT), where A is a constant, Ea is activation energy, R is gas constant, and T is temperature. By reducing the ΔT across cells from 15°C to <2°C, the capacity fade rate variance decreases by ~70% (calculated from Arrhenius equation with Ea=80 kJ/mol for NMC-811). This directly reduces the driving mechanism of imbalance drift, as cells age more uniformly.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL
Standard practice components:
- Copper busbars connecting cells in series
- 1 A balancing circuit
- Thermal interface material (TIM) between cells and module housing

Intervention components:
- (a) Replace standard copper busbars with thermally-enhanced busbars (same dimensions, same mounting points)
- (b) Add thermal vias (standard copper-plated via array, procured from PCB suppliers)
- (c) Modify busbar manufacturing process to incorporate thermal vias during fabrication
- (a) Maintain existing 1 A balancing circuit
- (a) Maintain existing TIM between cells and module housing

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY)
- Thermal busbars: same weight and volume as standard busbars (copper mass unchanged)
- Thermal vias: minimal additional mass (<5g per busbar, negligible in module context)
- Manufacturing change: requires new tooling for busbar stamping (one-time setup cost)
- No additional power consumption
- No increase in module footprint
- No additional maintenance procedures
Conclusion: Same burden class as standard practice. The intervention uses existing materials in modified configuration, with no increase in system complexity or ongoing operational costs.

EXECUTABLE TEST
Protocol: 
1. Build two identical 13-cell modules - one with standard busbars, one with thermal-enhanced busbars
2. Subject both modules to accelerated aging: 1C charge/discharge cycles at 40°C ambient with 15°C imposed thermal gradient
3. Monitor cell voltages and temperatures continuously
4. Measure cell capacity every 500 cycles
5. Test duration: 3000 cycles (equivalent to ~10 years calendar life)
6. Kill criterion: Any cell exceeds 35 mV voltage spread from average

Pass/fail threshold:
- Intervention module maintains <20 mV cell-to-cell voltage spread at all times
- Intervention module shows <15% capacity variation between cells after 3000 cycles
- Control module exceeds 35 mV spread before 3000 cycles

Effectiveness validation: The intervention is validated if the thermal-enhanced module maintains voltage spread below threshold throughout testing while the control module fails before test completion.
